summary: Defines a way to carry SMTP Message Transfer Priority values through mail transfer agents that do not support the MT-PRIORITY extension. This lets the priority survive hops that would otherwise drop it. It is informational and not an Internet Standards Track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: If some post offices ignore a rush sticker, you can hide the rush note inside the envelope so the next office still sees it.

questions: how to tunnel smtp mt-priority through old mail servers
subtitle: How to preserve email priority through mail servers that don't understand priority.

tldr.problem: The SMTP Message Transfer Priorities extension allows mail servers to prioritize delivery, but only works if all servers in the path support it. When a message passes through a server that does not support the extension, the priority information is lost.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines an MT-Priority header field that mail servers can add to a message body when forwarding to a non-supporting server. When the message reaches a supporting server again, it can extract the priority from the header field and resume prioritized handling.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can deploy message transfer priorities progressively without waiting for all mail servers to support the SMTP extension, enabling earlier benefits of priority-based mail routing.

today: RFC 6758 is an Informational document that extends the MT-PRIORITY mechanism from RFC 6710. The header field tunneling approach allows gradual deployment of message priorities in mail systems without requiring simultaneous support across the entire mail chain. The MT-Priority header field was registered with IANA as a permanent message header field.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6710 defines the Message Transfer Priorities SMTP extension (MT-PRIORITY), which allows mail clients and servers to mark messages with a priority level. Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs) and Message Submission Agents (MSAs) can then provide preferential handling to high-priority messages, such as expedited delivery or queue ordering.

However, like all SMTP extensions, MT-PRIORITY only works if every MTA in the delivery path supports it. When a message must be relayed through an MTA that does not support MT-PRIORITY, the priority information attached to the MAIL FROM command is lost, and downstream MTAs that do support the extension have no way to know the original priority.

This RFC solves that problem by defining a mechanism to tunnel priority information through unsupporting MTAs using a new message header field, allowing progressive deployment of message transfer priorities.
sections.plainLanguage: Some email servers understand "this is urgent". Others don't. This memo explains how to write "this is urgent" in the message itself so servers that don't understand the urgent flag can still pass the message to servers that do.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC addresses two main deployment scenarios. First, an MT-PRIORITY-capable mail client sends to a non-MT-PRIORITY Message Submission Agent (MSA), which forwards to an MT-PRIORITY-capable MTA. The MSA is the bottleneck: it cannot pass the priority to the MTA using the SMTP extension.

Second, an older mail client sends to an MT-PRIORITY-capable MSA, but the client cannot set the SMTP MT-PRIORITY parameter because its API only exposes message headers, not protocol parameters. In both cases, neither standard SMTP parameters nor waiting for full deployment would help.

The header field tunneling mechanism allows mail clients and servers to transmit priority even when upstream hops do not support the SMTP extension, enabling priority-based routing decisions at each supporting hop along the path.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes your email program can't tell the server "this is urgent" (the technical way), but it can write it inside the message. Sometimes the server you send to doesn't understand the technical way, so you write it in the message instead.

sections.title: The MT-Priority Header Field
sections.content:
The MT-Priority header field carries a priority value in the same format as the SMTP MT-PRIORITY parameter. The syntax is MT-Priority: -3 (for lowest priority) through MT-Priority: 4 (for highest priority), optionally followed by a policy name in parentheses, such as MT-Priority: 4 (ultra).

When an MTA receives a message without an explicit MT-PRIORITY MAIL FROM parameter, it checks for a syntactically valid MT-Priority header field. If found, it treats that value as the message's priority. When relaying to a non-MT-PRIORITY-capable MTA, the receiving MTA first removes any existing MT-Priority header fields, then adds a new one with the determined priority. This ensures only one valid MT-Priority header exists at any point.
sections.plainLanguage: The header field is a simple line that says the priority level, like "MT-Priority: 3". Each server reads it, uses it, and rewrites it for the next server if needed.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
When an MTA receives a message, it determines priority in order: first, the SMTP MT-PRIORITY MAIL FROM parameter (if present); second, a valid MT-Priority header field (if present); third, legacy headers like Priority or X-Priority (which may be used but are not preferred).

The Importance header field MUST NOT be used for determining priority, as it has different semantics and is intended for the end user recipient rather than mail transfer nodes.

When relaying to another conforming MT-PRIORITY-aware MTA, the standard SMTP parameter is used. When relaying to a non-conforming MTA, the receiving MTA must remove any MT-Priority headers and add a new one based on the determined priority, ensuring the priority survives the hop without protocol-level support.
sections.plainLanguage: Each server asks: did the sender tell me the priority (the technical way)? If not, is there a header field? If not, use the old-style headers? Use whichever one exists, in that order.

sections.title: Security Concerns
sections.content:
Allowing clients to set message priority creates potential abuse vectors. A malicious client could request priority 9 (highest) for all messages, overwhelming the mail system. MSAs and MTAs MUST authenticate and authorize users before accepting MT-PRIORITY parameters or headers, restricting priority values based on user policy.

The MT-Priority header field should be protected using DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) or S/MIME signatures to verify that a trusted agent set the priority. If an MSA or MTA receives a DKIM-signed message with an MT-Priority header and needs to change the priority due to policy, it faces a dilemma: changing the header breaks the DKIM signature. The RFC recommends carefully considering deployment policies and re-signing messages with DKIM when modifying headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad people could lie and say everything is urgent. Email servers need to check who is asking and only let trusted senders use high priority. Also, if someone signed the message, changing the priority ruins the signature.
